title: Chunk serialization impact: latency & cost lab notes
body:
Purpose
This note captures early lab results comparing chunk/response serialization formats and parameters for streaming chat responses. We want to quantify network+CPU serialization overhead that shows up in p50/p90/p99 at the service edge and how those translate into per-token cost when measured on our hosted API profile (m-13b quantized, 8xA100-like endpoints).

Quick summary (top-level takeaways)
- Serialization format materially affects tail latency: text-based JSON line-delimited streaming adds ~8–18% p90 overhead vs compact binary formats for small chunk sizes (<512B).
- Chunk size is a dominant knob: increasing chunk payload from 256B->2KB reduces p99 by ~20–35% for all formats due to fewer write/syscall/flush events.
- Compression (gzip) reduces bytes on the wire by 40–65% but often increases p50 by 5–12ms when gzip runs on the worker thread; CPU-bound workers show larger penalties. Offloading compression to a separate thread/process reduces that penalty but adds complexity.
- Cost impact (hosted API unit economics): with typical request mix (mean response 150 tokens), the incremental network+CPU cost from JSON streaming vs protobuf is ~+$0.002–0.007 per 1k requests (depending on chunkization), which aggregates to nontrivial monthly spend at scale.

Methodology (how we ran it)
- Workload: synthetic chat requests derived from real customer prompts (anonymized), mean model output 150 tokens, stdev 90 tokens (heavy tail).
- Model: m-13b-quant (our internal staging config).
- Cluster: dedicated dev pool (8 x A100-class equivalent) behind load-gen machine colocated in same AZ.
- Client: simple streaming consumer that records first-chunk latency, last-chunk latency, and inter-chunk gaps. Each configuration ran 5 stable runs of 10k requests (ramp 60s, steady 5m).
- Measured: p50/p90/p99 end-to-end server-to-client observed latency, server CPU utilization, network bytes, and per-request serialization CPU time sampled via perf counters.

Configurations tested
- Formats: line-delimited JSON (text), CBOR (compact binary), Protobuf (length-prefixed), custom msgpack, and JSON+gzip.
- Chunk sizes: target body payload per chunk: 256B, 512B, 1KB, 2KB, and an un-chunked / full-frame mode (single write at completion).
- Flush policy: immediate (write after each token batch), coalesce 50ms, coalesce 200ms.

Representative numbers (median of 5 runs)
Note: numbers are device-edge observed (includes serialization + network transfer to client in same AZ), p50/p90/p99 in milliseconds. Throughput is effective completed reqs/sec at steady state. Cost delta is incremental network+CPU unit cost approximated from our internal cost model (USD per 1M tokens).

ASCII table: format | chunk | p50(ms) | p90(ms) | p99(ms) | throughput(req/s) | net bytes/req | cost-delta($/1M tokens)
JSON (text)   | 256B  | 105     | 240     | 760     | 420              | 5.8 KB       |  +4.8
CBOR (binary) | 256B  | 95      | 210     | 620     | 450              | 4.9 KB       |  +3.1
Protobuf      | 256B  | 88      | 180     | 540     | 480              | 4.5 KB       |  +2.6
MessagePack   | 256B  | 92      | 190     | 560     | 470              | 4.6 KB       |  +2.8
JSON+gzip     | 256B  | 120     | 260     | 820     | 390              | 2.6 KB       |  +5.4

Same but 2KB chunk size:
JSON (text)   | 2KB   | 85      | 170     | 520     | 520              | 7.2 KB       |  +3.6
CBOR (binary) | 2KB   | 80      | 150     | 420     | 560              | 6.3 KB       |  +2.2
Protobuf      | 2KB   | 75      | 138     | 380     | 600              | 6.1 KB       |  +1.9
MessagePack   | 2KB   | 77      | 142     | 400     | 590              | 6.2 KB       |  +2.0
JSON+gzip     | 2KB   | 90      | 185     | 480     | 540              | 3.1 KB       |  +3.8

Interpretation notes
- Why JSON is slower: text encoding per token is CPU-inefficient and causes larger write syscalls per chunk due to quotes/escaping. The runtime spends ~0.7–1.5ms extra per 256B chunk serializing to JSON vs protobuf. That accumulates on small-chunk heavy streams.
- Why protobuf/CBOR win: smaller encoded size and faster native serializers (C++ optimized path) reduce CPU time and allow higher throughput on the same instance.
- Compression tradeoffs: gz reduces bytes substantially but gzip CPU cost is nontrivial; net improvement only when network is the bottleneck (e.g., cross-region or client on mobile with limited link). For same-AZ traffic, gzip often hurts latency.
- Flush/coalesce policy matters: coalescing with a 50ms window reduces p99 more than switching format for small responses. However, coalescing increases observed first-chunk latency (bad for streaming UX).

Chart (text) — p99 vs chunk-size by format (units ms):
Chunk-size (B):    256    512    1024    2048
JSON p99 (ms):     760    680    610     520
Protobuf p99 (ms): 540    480    430     380
CBOR p99 (ms):     620    540    470     420

Operational implications for product choices
- Hosted default: recommend protobuf streaming with 1KB chunk target + optional 50ms coalesce for most public API endpoints where latency SLO is p90<200ms and streaming freshness is less critical. This balances tail latency and server CPU.
- Client SDKs: provide built-in CBOR/Protobuf decoders in JS/Go with a fallback to JSON for compatibility. Defaulting to text JSON currently hurts tail latency for high-volume apps.
- Compression: enable gzip at the edge only for cross-region or known high-latency networks. Add a runtime knob on per-client basis and instrument network bottleneck detection to auto-enable.
- Dedicated/private: for on-prem/private customers with constrained network (edge devices), gzip may be net-positive; recommend enabling but profiling is required.

Open questions / follow-ups
- Need to quantify impact on server-side memory alloc patterns (we saw increased allocator churn for JSON in some runs). File an infra perf ticket to heap-scan top alloc sites.
- Evaluate zero-copy serializers (flatbuffers) and link with JNI/Node add-ons to reduce JS-path overhead.
- Client UX tradeoff: first-chunk latency vs p99 savings from coalesce — run small A/B with real customers.
- Cost model precision: current cost deltas are rough; re-run with billing-model inputs post Q2 pricing update.

Immediate action items
- (OBS-2314) Add protobuf streaming as an opt-in in the JS SDK (Markus).
- Add a 1KB default chunk-target and 50ms coalesce policy to runtime staging (Sofia) and re-run the benchmark with per-endpoint traces.
- Create an infra perf ticket for allocator churn (Diego).

Appendix: raw samples and logs
- Attached: sample traces recorded (trace-ids) and aggregated perf counters; see linked artifacts for the PR + linear ticket.
- Example trace snippet (first-chunk times, 256B JSON):
  req-0001: first-chunk 34ms, last-chunk 420ms, total 480ms, serialized-bytes 6.1KB
  req-0002: first-chunk 29ms, last-chunk 530ms, total 610ms, serialized-bytes 5.7KB

Notes to reviewers
- This is exploratory benching; numbers will shift with model family and infra generation. Focus review on comparative deltas (format vs chunk-size) not absolute latency numbers.
- Prefer to ship pragmatic SDK defaults rather than forcing JSON everywhere.
